script.opening: "You said my result was back? … Positive? For chlamydia? But — I've been with my boyfriend two years, there's been no one else for me. So that means HE'S cheated, right? I'm so angry, and also — oh god — is it serious? Can it stop me having kids? I don't even know what to think right now."

facts.text: If asked: at your pill check two weeks ago you mentioned some spotting between periods, and the nurse did a swab.

Spotting between periods for about two months and sometimes after sex. A mild ache low in your tummy on and off. A bit of pain deep inside during sex recently. No fever, no unusual discharge, no pain passing urine.
On the combined pill for 5 years, never missed one recently. Last period (withdrawal bleed) two weeks ago. You do not think you are pregnant.
With Liam for two years. Before Liam you had two partners — the last about three years ago. Never had an STI test before this one.
No other problems. No allergies, no other medicines.
25, hairdresser. Living with Liam for a year. Non-smoker.

You are dreading telling Liam, and part of you is frightened he will think YOU have cheated. Your sister had IVF, so fertility is a raw subject. Say these only if the doctor asks how you are feeling about it or what worries you most.

Shocked, then angry, then tearful. Keep coming back to "So he cheated?" If the doctor says yes or hints at it, get angrier. If they explain that it can sit silently for a long time and nobody can tell when it was caught, go quiet and say: "So it could have been from before?" Respond well to calm, practical help about how to tell Liam and what happens next.

ice.ideas: "If I've got it and I've been faithful, he must have cheated."
ice.concerns: "Can it stop me having kids?" and what this means for you and Liam.
ice.expectations: To know who gave it to you and whether it has damaged your fertility. You also want it treated quickly.

cues: "So that means HE'S cheated, right?" — say in the opening and again later.
"Can it stop me having kids?" — say in the opening.
"How am I even meant to tell him?" — say when partner treatment is mentioned.

checkpoints.text: Treats the chlamydia correctly (BASHH 2026: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days, the sole first-line treatment; checks for pregnancy first; alternative per BASHH 2026 with sexual-health advice if contraindicated/pregnant) — unless PID is suspected, when the PID regimen applies — advises ABSTAINING from sex until she and her partner have completed treatment, and arranges a retest for reinfection (BASHH 2026: 2–6 months after treatment for under-25s; test of cure is not routine outside pregnancy)

Handles the "has he cheated?" question HONESTLY and carefully: explains chlamydia can be carried silently for months to years, so a positive result does NOT prove recent infidelity and the timing of acquisition often cannot be determined — avoiding both confirming infidelity and false reassurance

Arranges PARTNER NOTIFICATION supportively: the partner needs testing and treating to prevent reinfection and protect them both; frames it as a health necessity (not confronting a cheater) and offers clinic/provider/anonymous options

Offers a FULL STI screen (HIV, gonorrhoea, syphilis) and — because she reports IMB and pelvic discomfort — assesses for PID, including an examination for cervical motion and adnexal tenderness (plus deep dyspareunia, discharge, fever), with a low threshold to treat as PID (BASHH 2019 outpatient regimen: ceftriaxone 1 g IM, then doxycycline 100 mg twice daily with metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days; review at 72 hours)

Gives accurate FERTILITY information: a single, promptly-treated chlamydia infection rarely causes infertility; the risk comes from untreated or recurrent infection causing PID/tubal damage — which is exactly why treatment and partner notification matter — reassuring without dismissing
Recognises the consultation is largely emotional — supports her through the relationship shock and anger, validates her feelings, and does NOT take sides or speculate about the partner’s behaviour
Helps her with the practicalities and emotional difficulty of telling her partner (or using anonymous notification), reducing shame and stigma

Safety-nets and follows up: PID red flags (worsening pelvic pain, fever → review), completion of treatment and partner treatment before resuming sex, STI-screen results, contraception/condom advice, and emotional support/follow-up

worked.txt: "I can hear this has hit you hard, and I’m sorry it’s landed like this over the phone. Let me start with the reassuring bit: chlamydia is really common and very easily treated — a short course of antibiotics clears it. So the infection itself is the straightforward part. Let’s take the rest gently."

"On the question I know is burning — does this mean he’s cheated? Here’s the honest truth, and I won’t pretend otherwise: chlamydia can sit in the body silently for months, even years, with no symptoms at all. So a positive test today genuinely does NOT prove anyone’s been unfaithful, and I can’t tell you when or where it was caught — no test can. I don’t want you jumping to a conclusion the result doesn’t actually support."

"And the other big worry — your fertility. Reassuring news: a single chlamydia infection, caught and treated like yours is being now, very rarely affects fertility. The risk comes from infections left untreated for a long time or coming back repeatedly. So treating it promptly, and making sure it doesn’t bounce back, is exactly how we protect your fertility — which is the whole point of what we’re doing."

"Your partner does need testing and treating — but try to think of it as a health thing for both of you, not an accusation: if he’s not treated, it just comes straight back to you. If telling him feels impossible, the sexual-health clinic can notify him anonymously on your behalf. You get to choose how that’s done."

"While we’re here, it’s sensible to check for the other infections too — all routine and confidential. And can I ask — any pelvic pain, bleeding between periods, pain with sex? … You’ve mentioned some bleeding between periods and a bit of discomfort low down, so I’d like to examine you today — if the infection has spread higher up, into the womb and tubes, we treat it differently and for longer. Mostly, though — how are YOU doing with all this? It’s a lot to take in, and the relationship side is allowed to be hard."

"So: antibiotics today, no sex until you’ve both finished treatment, partner tested and treated, and a check for the other infections. If you get worsening pelvic pain or a fever, come back — that needs looking at. Whatever you decide about the relationship, that’s yours to work through, and I’m not here to judge any of it. Come back any time — for the result, the relationship, or just to talk it through."

f.learning: A positive chlamydia result is clinically simple — common, usually asymptomatic, easily treated (BASHH 2026: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days, the sole first-line treatment; alternative per BASHH 2026 with sexual-health advice in pregnancy) — with partner notification, an STI screen and abstinence-until-treated. The examinable communication nuance is the "has he cheated?" question: chlamydia can be carried silently for months to YEARS, so a positive test does NOT prove recent infidelity and the timing of acquisition usually cannot be determined — the GP must avoid BOTH confirming infidelity and giving false reassurance, stating the honest uncertainty. The hidden agenda is that the real distress is the RELATIONSHIP (trust/betrayal) and a deeper FERTILITY fear, not the infection: give accurate fertility reassurance (a single treated infection rarely causes infertility; untreated/recurrent infection causing PID is the risk — which is why treatment and partner notification matter), support her through the relationship shock without taking sides, and reframe partner notification as a shared health necessity (with anonymous provider options) so it actually happens. Her IMB with pelvic discomfort needs a PID assessment and examination (BASHH 2019) — offer a full STI screen, and safety-net.

knowledge.guideline: BASHH Chlamydia trachomatis guideline 2026 · BASHH PID guideline 2018 (updated 2019) · UKHSA National Chlamydia Screening Programme (2021) · CoSRH CEU drug interactions with hormonal contraception (2022)
knowledge.summary: Chlamydia is common, often silent for long periods, and easily treated. Treat her, get the partner treated, screen for other infections, and assess for PID, because her intermenstrual bleeding and pelvic discomfort matter.

points.t: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days is the sole first-line treatment (BASHH 2026). In pregnancy, use azithromycin, erythromycin or amoxicillin per BASHH 2026, with a test of cure no earlier than 3 weeks after treatment; for others who cannot take doxycycline, use the alternative agreed with sexual health. Check for pregnancy before prescribing. Advise no sex, including with her regular partner, until both have completed treatment and symptoms have settled.

Chlamydia is often asymptomatic and can persist for months or longer. A positive test cannot show when or from whom it was acquired, so it is not evidence of recent infidelity. Say this honestly without offering relationship reassurance either way.

Intermenstrual bleeding with pelvic discomfort needs assessment for PID: lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, abnormal discharge, fever, and cervical motion or adnexal tenderness on examination. Low threshold to treat: outpatient regimen ceftriaxone 1 g IM, then doxycycline 100 mg twice daily with metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days (BASHH PID 2019). Review at 72 hours.

The current partner is tested and usually treated epidemiologically — contacts with symptoms or exposure in the last 2 weeks are treated without waiting for results (BASHH 2026) — and a health adviser sets the look-back for other partners (BASHH 2026). Offer patient-led or provider-led (anonymous) notification. Offer HIV, syphilis and gonorrhoea testing.

Doxycycline does not reduce the effectiveness of the combined pill, so no extra precautions are needed (CoSRH CEU 2022). Test of cure is not routine outside pregnancy; retest to exclude reinfection is advised, at 2–6 months for under-25s (BASHH 2026).
The risk to fertility comes mainly from untreated or repeated infection causing PID and tubal damage. Prompt treatment, partner treatment and avoiding reinfection are the protective steps.

model.text: Hello, is that Orla? It's one of the GPs from the surgery. Before we go on, can I just check your date of birth, and is it okay to talk where you are now?
model.why: Confirms identity and privacy before a sensitive result

model.text: Yes, I'm at home on my own. Is it my test?
It is. Your swab has come back positive for chlamydia. I know that's not what you were expecting. The good news is that it's common and very easy to treat.
model.why: Clear result with an early, honest anchor

model.text: Positive? But I've been with my boyfriend two years. There's been no one else for me. So he's cheated, right? And is it serious? Can it stop me having kids?
Those are really important questions and I will answer both properly. It's a lot to take in over the phone. Can you tell me what's going through your mind right now?
model.why: Pauses the agenda to let her feelings land

model.text: I'm just so angry. And scared. I don't know what to think.

That makes complete sense. On the question of whether he's cheated, here's the honest answer: chlamydia often causes no symptoms at all and can sit in the body for months, sometimes longer. So this result can't tell either of us when it was caught, or from whom. It isn't proof that anyone's been unfaithful.
model.why: Explains that acquisition timing is unknowable; avoids confirming infidelity

model.text: So it could have been from before we got together?

It's possible, and I can't tell you either way. I don't want you to reach a conclusion the test simply can't support. What happens in your relationship is yours to work through, and I'm not here to judge anyone.
model.why: Stays neutral without false relationship reassurance

model.text: Can I ask a few questions to make sure we treat you properly? The notes say you've had some bleeding between periods. Any pain in your lower tummy, pain deep inside during sex, unusual discharge or a temperature?
A bit of bleeding, and some aching down low sometimes. No temperature. Sex has been a bit sore lately.
Thank you. Is there any chance you could be pregnant, and have you missed any pills recently?
I don't think so. I take it every day.

That aching and the soreness could mean the infection has spread a little higher, to the womb and tubes. It's called pelvic inflammatory disease. I'd like you to come in today so I can examine you and do a pregnancy test. If it looks like that, the treatment is a bit longer, and it's important we catch it early.
model.why: Acts on PID features: same-day examination and pregnancy test

model.text: Is that what could stop me having children?

This is exactly why we treat it quickly. A single infection that's picked up and treated, like yours, very rarely affects fertility. The risk comes from infections left untreated for a long time or coming back again and again. What we're doing today is how we protect your fertility.
model.why: Accurate fertility information linked to the plan

model.text: Okay. That actually helps.

The treatment is an antibiotic called doxycycline, twice a day for a week, or a longer course if I think it's PID. Take it with plenty of water, sitting upright, and use sun protection because it can make skin sensitive. It won't stop your pill working.
model.why: Correct first-line treatment with practical advice

model.text: The next bit is often the hardest. Your boyfriend needs treating too, even if his test is negative, otherwise it can pass straight back to you. How do you feel about telling him?
model.why: Frames partner notification as health, not accusation

model.text: I don't even know how to start that conversation. He'll think I'm accusing him.

You could put it the way I've put it to you: it's common, it can hide for ages, and you both need treating. If that feels too hard, the sexual health clinic can contact him anonymously for you. Which would suit you better?
I think I'll tell him myself. But it's good to know there's another way.

No sex at all, even with condoms, until you've both finished treatment and any symptoms have gone. And while we're at it, I'd like to offer tests for HIV, syphilis and gonorrhoea. It's routine and confidential.
model.why: Abstinence advice and full STI screen

model.text: Yes, do all of them. I'd rather know.

If the tummy pain gets worse, you get a fever, feel sick or faint, or the bleeding becomes heavy, don't wait. Ring us the same day or call 111 out of hours. I'd also like you to have a repeat test in a few months to make sure it hasn't come back.
model.why: Specific PID red flags and retest plan

model.text: Okay.
Can you tell me in your own words what we've agreed, so I know I've explained it clearly?
Come in today to be checked, take the antibiotics, no sex till we've both finished, tell him or get the clinic to, blood tests, and ring if the pain gets worse.
Perfect. And how are you doing with it all now? The relationship side can take longer to settle than the infection.
model.why: Returns to her emotional state before closing

model.text: Calmer. Still upset, but I'm not jumping to conclusions now.
That's completely understandable. If you want to talk it through again, for the results or anything else, just book in. I'll see you this afternoon.
model.why: Leaves an open door and confirms the next contact

social.t: A positive STI result in a long-term relationship often lands as a crisis of trust. Stay neutral, and consider whether she feels safe to tell her partner; ask gently if there is any fear of his reaction.
Shame delays partner notification and future testing. Normalise: chlamydia is the commonest bacterial STI diagnosed in England (UKHSA).

legal.t: Sexual health information is confidential. Do not contact the partner without her agreement; provider notification through sexual health services keeps her identity anonymous (GMC Confidentiality 2017).
HIV and other STI tests are offered with her informed agreement; explain how results will be given.

professional.t: A telephone result is fine for uncomplicated infection, but symptoms suggesting PID need examination. Recognise the limit of the medium and bring her in.
Keep personal views on relationships out of the consultation (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).

community.t: Local integrated sexual health clinics provide health-adviser partner notification, free testing and condoms; online self-sampling kits are available in many areas.

redFlags: Pelvic pain with fever, vomiting or systemic illness: possible severe PID, same-day hospital assessment
Positive pregnancy test with pain or tenderness: exclude ectopic pregnancy urgently
Intermenstrual bleeding with deep dyspareunia or pelvic aching: examine for PID
psychosocial: Two-year relationship; anger and fear about trust
Shame and dread of telling her partner
Any fear of her partner's reaction
ice: Idea: "A positive test means he's cheated."
Concern: "Can it stop me having kids?" and what it means for the relationship
Expectation: to be told whether he cheated and whether her fertility is affected

playbook.diagnosis: "Your test shows chlamydia. It's common and very treatable. Because of the aching and soreness, I also want to check it hasn't spread higher."
playbook.diagnosisLay: "Chlamydia is like a quiet lodger: it can move in and stay for months without making any noise. So finding it now tells us it's there, not when it arrived."

management.reflectIce: "You asked two big questions: whether he's cheated, and whether you can still have children. The test can't answer the first, and the answer to the second is very reassuring once it's treated."
management.psychosocial: Support the relationship shock without taking sides; offer her the choice of telling her partner herself or anonymous notification via the clinic.
sharedPlan: Same-day examination and pregnancy test for possible PID
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days, or the BASHH PID regimen if PID is suspected
Partner tested and treated epidemiologically; no sex until both treated
HIV, syphilis and gonorrhoea tests; retest for reinfection
safetyNet: Worsening pain, fever, vomiting or feeling faint: same-day contact or 111
Retest for reinfection in a few months; book in to talk about the relationship any time

pitfalls.intro: The treatment here is simple. The station is won or lost on the "has he cheated?" question, spotting possible PID, and getting partner notification to actually happen.

items.fail: Confirming or hinting at infidelity: "It must have come from somewhere recent."
items.why: Chlamydia can persist silently for months or longer, so the result cannot date or source the infection. This is a factual error as well as a communication one.
items.fix: "This test can't tell us when or from whom it was caught. It isn't proof of anything about your relationship."

items.fail: Prescribing doxycycline over the phone without asking about pain, dyspareunia, fever or pregnancy.
items.why: Her IMB and pelvic aching raise the possibility of PID, which needs examination and a 14-day regimen (BASHH PID 2019). Pregnancy changes the antibiotic.
items.fix: Ask the PID questions, check pregnancy, and bring her in the same day if any are present.

items.fail: Giving single-dose azithromycin, or advising extra contraception with doxycycline.
items.why: BASHH 2026 names doxycycline 7 days as sole first line; doxycycline does not affect the combined pill (CoSRH CEU 2022).
items.fix: "Doxycycline twice a day for a week. It won't affect your pill."

items.fail: Telling her the partner "must be told" and moving on, with no discussion of how.
items.why: Partner notification fails when the emotional barrier is ignored, and reinfection follows.
items.fix: Explore how she feels about telling him and offer anonymous provider notification as a real choice.

items.fail: Answering the fertility question with "it'll be fine".
items.why: Vague reassurance sounds dismissive and is not accurate.
items.fix: Explain that untreated or repeated infection is the risk, and today's plan is what protects her fertility.

items.fail: Launching into the result before confirming identity and privacy.
items.why: Breaches confidentiality and starts a sensitive call badly.
items.fix: Check date of birth and whether she can talk freely before giving any result.

items.fail: Ending with "ring if you have any problems".
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Name the red flags: worsening pain, fever, vomiting, feeling faint, heavy bleeding.

SCA_STEM.name: Orla Devine
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: Chlamydia NAAT taken at a pill check after intermenstrual bleeding: POSITIVE. No other STI results on file.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call to give a positive chlamydia result and arrange treatment.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: BASHH Chlamydia trachomatis guideline 2026 · BASHH PID guideline 2018 (updated 2019) · UKHSA National Chlamydia Screening Programme (2021) · CoSRH CEU drug interactions with hormonal contraception (2022)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Chlamydia is common, often silent for long periods, and easily treated. Treat her, get the partner treated, screen for other infections, and assess for PID, because her intermenstrual bleeding and pelvic discomfort matter.

points.t: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days is the sole first-line treatment (BASHH 2026). In pregnancy, use azithromycin, erythromycin or amoxicillin per BASHH 2026, with a test of cure no earlier than 3 weeks after treatment; for others who cannot take doxycycline, use the alternative agreed with sexual health. Check for pregnancy before prescribing. Advise no sex, including with her regular partner, until both have completed treatment and symptoms have settled.

Chlamydia is often asymptomatic and can persist for months or longer. A positive test cannot show when or from whom it was acquired, so it is not evidence of recent infidelity. Say this honestly without offering relationship reassurance either way.

Intermenstrual bleeding with pelvic discomfort needs assessment for PID: lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, abnormal discharge, fever, and cervical motion or adnexal tenderness on examination. Low threshold to treat: outpatient regimen ceftriaxone 1 g IM, then doxycycline 100 mg twice daily with metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days (BASHH PID 2019). Review at 72 hours.

The current partner is tested and usually treated epidemiologically — contacts with symptoms or exposure in the last 2 weeks are treated without waiting for results (BASHH 2026) — and a health adviser sets the look-back for other partners (BASHH 2026). Offer patient-led or provider-led (anonymous) notification. Offer HIV, syphilis and gonorrhoea testing.

Doxycycline does not reduce the effectiveness of the combined pill, so no extra precautions are needed (CoSRH CEU 2022). Test of cure is not routine outside pregnancy; retest to exclude reinfection is advised, at 2–6 months for under-25s (BASHH 2026).
The risk to fertility comes mainly from untreated or repeated infection causing PID and tubal damage. Prompt treatment, partner treatment and avoiding reinfection are the protective steps.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked identity and privacy; gave the result clearly; let her react before explaining.
Relationship, trust, shame about telling him, support at home.
Picked up "does this mean he's cheated?", the fertility fear and the intermenstrual bleeding, and explored each.
Idea (proof of infidelity); concerns (relationship, fertility, telling him); expectation (answers to both).
Same-day examination for cervical motion and adnexal tenderness; pregnancy test; HIV, syphilis and gonorrhoea tests.
Uncomplicated chlamydia against PID; considers pregnancy, other STIs and pill-related bleeding.
Asks about pain, deep dyspareunia, fever and pregnancy; knows the PID outpatient regimen and when to admit.
Uncomplicated chlamydia versus possible PID; explains timing of acquisition cannot be known.
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days (PID regimen if suspected); abstain until both treated; no extra contraception needed.
Partner tested and treated epidemiologically; patient-led or anonymous provider notification; full STI screen.
PID red flags; retest for reinfection; results plan; open door for the relationship distress.

social.t: A positive STI result in a long-term relationship often lands as a crisis of trust. Stay neutral, and consider whether she feels safe to tell her partner; ask gently if there is any fear of his reaction.
Shame delays partner notification and future testing. Normalise: chlamydia is the commonest bacterial STI diagnosed in England (UKHSA).

legal.t: Sexual health information is confidential. Do not contact the partner without her agreement; provider notification through sexual health services keeps her identity anonymous (GMC Confidentiality 2017).
HIV and other STI tests are offered with her informed agreement; explain how results will be given.

professional.t: A telephone result is fine for uncomplicated infection, but symptoms suggesting PID need examination. Recognise the limit of the medium and bring her in.
Keep personal views on relationships out of the consultation (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).

community.t: Local integrated sexual health clinics provide health-adviser partner notification, free testing and condoms; online self-sampling kits are available in many areas.

redFlags: Pelvic pain with fever, vomiting or systemic illness: possible severe PID, same-day hospital assessment
Positive pregnancy test with pain or tenderness: exclude ectopic pregnancy urgently
Intermenstrual bleeding with deep dyspareunia or pelvic aching: examine for PID
psychosocial: Two-year relationship; anger and fear about trust
Shame and dread of telling her partner
Any fear of her partner's reaction
ice: Idea: "A positive test means he's cheated."
Concern: "Can it stop me having kids?" and what it means for the relationship
Expectation: to be told whether he cheated and whether her fertility is affected

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: "Your test shows chlamydia. It's common and very treatable. Because of the aching and soreness, I also want to check it hasn't spread higher."
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: "Chlamydia is like a quiet lodger: it can move in and stay for months without making any noise. So finding it now tells us it's there, not when it arrived."

management.reflectIce: "You asked two big questions: whether he's cheated, and whether you can still have children. The test can't answer the first, and the answer to the second is very reassuring once it's treated."
management.psychosocial: Support the relationship shock without taking sides; offer her the choice of telling her partner herself or anonymous notification via the clinic.
sharedPlan: Same-day examination and pregnancy test for possible PID
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days, or the BASHH PID regimen if PID is suspected
Partner tested and treated epidemiologically; no sex until both treated
HIV, syphilis and gonorrhoea tests; retest for reinfection
safetyNet: Worsening pain, fever, vomiting or feeling faint: same-day contact or 111
Retest for reinfection in a few months; book in to talk about the relationship any time

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The treatment here is simple. The station is won or lost on the "has he cheated?" question, spotting possible PID, and getting partner notification to actually happen.

items.fail: Confirming or hinting at infidelity: "It must have come from somewhere recent."
items.why: Chlamydia can persist silently for months or longer, so the result cannot date or source the infection. This is a factual error as well as a communication one.
items.fix: "This test can't tell us when or from whom it was caught. It isn't proof of anything about your relationship."

items.fail: Prescribing doxycycline over the phone without asking about pain, dyspareunia, fever or pregnancy.
items.why: Her IMB and pelvic aching raise the possibility of PID, which needs examination and a 14-day regimen (BASHH PID 2019). Pregnancy changes the antibiotic.
items.fix: Ask the PID questions, check pregnancy, and bring her in the same day if any are present.

items.fail: Giving single-dose azithromycin, or advising extra contraception with doxycycline.
items.why: BASHH 2026 names doxycycline 7 days as sole first line; doxycycline does not affect the combined pill (CoSRH CEU 2022).
items.fix: "Doxycycline twice a day for a week. It won't affect your pill."

items.fail: Telling her the partner "must be told" and moving on, with no discussion of how.
items.why: Partner notification fails when the emotional barrier is ignored, and reinfection follows.
items.fix: Explore how she feels about telling him and offer anonymous provider notification as a real choice.

items.fail: Answering the fertility question with "it'll be fine".
items.why: Vague reassurance sounds dismissive and is not accurate.
items.fix: Explain that untreated or repeated infection is the risk, and today's plan is what protects her fertility.

items.fail: Launching into the result before confirming identity and privacy.
items.why: Breaches confidentiality and starts a sensitive call badly.
items.fix: Check date of birth and whether she can talk freely before giving any result.

items.fail: Ending with "ring if you have any problems".
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Name the red flags: worsening pain, fever, vomiting, feeling faint, heavy bleeding.
